title: Norris on Brazilian GP pole as Russell rages at Mercedes over aborted lap
raw_summary: Lando Norris snatched a stunning Brazilian Grand Prix pole position at Interlagos in torrential rain, as George Russell felt Mercedes robbed him of a chance to finish first, despite a five-place grid penalty rendering that effectively irrelevant anyway. After rain delayed the start of F1 qualifying by an hour and 25 minutes, Q1 got underway and you could tell conditions were treacherous merely by the rarely used wet weather tyres being bolted onto all of the cars, while by the time Q3 rolled around it was dry enough for intermediates. But, and it was a big but, the weather radar suggested there would only be time for one flying lap before more heavy rain arrived early in Q3. In the end there was time for two laps, and Russell was fastest with the first, and then looked good enough to be quickest in the second before backing off at the end of his second lap when he caught Alex Albon's Williams. GR: "Move, Albono!" Merc: “So, we will get one more lap here.” Russell: “You need to tell me mate what I’m doing, if I’m backing or going.” Merc: “We can back up now, back up now.” Russell: “Are you sure?” Merc: “It’s raining heavier now.” [Russell prepares to start final lap] Merc: “It’s raining heavily now in the pitlane.” Russell: “Mate I should have f***ing finished the lap!” [Halfway round lap when it’s clear it’s done] Russell: “MATE! You f***ing told me to back off. What the hell!” Wolff: “George you’re P2" Russell: “Yeah but…P2. I don’t wanna be P2, I want to be P1. That was a P1 lap. F******ing hell!” The final gap was 0.204s, but it doesn't really matter as Russell will drop back five places for an engine penalty.

You f***ing told me to back off. What the hell!” Wolff: “George you’re P2" Russell: “Yeah but…P2. I don’t wanna be P2, I want to be P1. That was a P1 lap. F******ing hell!” The final gap was 0.204s, but it doesn't really matter as Russell will drop back five places for an engine penalty.

Norris has to be happy with a wet pole at Interlagos, a huge badge of honour for any driver and a reminder of his talent as the outgoing world champion. The champion elect, Kimi Antonelli, took third, ahead of Charles Leclerc's Ferrari - facing a 10-place grid penalty - and two of the stars of qualifying, Liam Lawson and Nico Hulkenberg who will start third and fourth after penalties. Lawson was the fastest initially on the inters in Q2, and delivered again in Q3 to take fifth for Racing Bulls. Will that be enough to sway a decision from Racing Bulls on keeping him in F1 next year? Hulkenberg was also spectacular and took sixth - rising to fourth on the grid after penalties are applied, which will be Audi's highest start - ahead of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull. Ollie Bearman and Fernando Alonso - his best start for Aston Martin this year - both impressed across qualifying to take eighth and ninth respectively, ahead of Alex Albon, who made Q3 for Williams.

Q2 produced plenty of drama as Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen went out, while rookie Rafael Camara crashed. Verstappen cleverly decided not to run in the session at all to save tyres for tomorrow's race and protect his car, owing to the back-of-the-grid penalty he'll serve tomorrow for an unscheduled engine change.

He had been third quickest in Q1. Hamilton did elect to run, but didn't switch to intermediates with six minutes to go like the rest of the field and sat in the pits in his Ferrari, basically surrendering the rest of the session for the same reasons as Verstappen, as Hamilton will also start at the back of the grid after an engine change. Camara's red flag effectively ended Q2 early. He locked up and went straight on at Juncao - a problem corner all session - and hit the barriers. He had also had a scrape in Q1 when he lost the car in a striaght line aquaplaning into the barrier on the Reta Oposta straight!

But Camara went from zero to hero by beating team-mate Ollie Bearman in Q1 - who also went off at Juncao late on in that session - and then took 13th in Q2 on his F1 debut. Just behind Hamilton was Oscar Piastri's McLaren, while Arvid Lindblad's Racing Bulls (which broke down on track) and Carlos Sainz's Williams were the other cars eliminated in Q2.

Despite the appalling conditions it was a relatively predictable Q1 exit list, apart from the two Alpines of Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto. Colapinto reported his tyres were done on the last lap and he then appeared to hold up Gasly behind, consigning both to a Q1 exit in that order. Despite Alonso regularly challenging towards the top and ending Q1 in eighth, Lance Stroll was only 19th via an early off at Juncao, ahead of Valtteri Bottas who was nearly seven tenths ahead of team-mate Sergio Perez, but Perez does have a grid penalty that will send him to the back of the grid. Gabriel Bortoleto anchored the order as he went off at Juncao and broke his rear wing, ending his session early.

title: REDD
raw_summary: REDD, the name for our new Tesla Model Y (Standard Range ’26 build, ’27 model), was inspired by the movie of the same name – Retired, Extremely Dangerous Drivers (the wife and I, of course). As mentioned previously, there is nothing wrong with our beloved 2019 Model 3. It is our bodies that are aging and less able to get in and out of our beloved little sporty Tess. article_paragraphs: REDD, the name for our new Tesla Model Y (Standard Range ’26 build, ’27 model), was inspired by the movie of the same name – Retired, Extremely Dangerous Drivers (the wife and I, of course). As mentioned previously, there is nothing wrong with our beloved 2019 Model 3. It is our bodies that are aging and less able to get in and out of our beloved little sporty Tess. So it was with mixed feelings that we arrived at the Tesla delivery centre to pick up the new car.

As always, it was a hive of activity, with deliveries taking place all around us. Quite a contrast to 7 years ago when Tesla was operating out of one cramped delivery spot near the centre of Brisbane, and the handover took less than 3 minutes. This time there were plenty of sales representatives spending their time and making sure we knew what we were doing.

On arrival, we walked past a line consisting of ICE cars being surrendered as trade-ins for an electric. As we left, a car carrier was unloading half a dozen new Model Ys. All in all, a smooth operation. While Majella was getting her phone synced and lots of information from the sales rep, I had a wander around.

The delivery centre is divided in two by a screen. On our side of the screen, I could see at least 60 new cars anxiously awaiting their new owners — like puppies at the pound, I thought. I wasn’t allowed behind the curtain where cars were being detailed and prepped. I commented to our sales rep that there didn’t seem to be many Model 3s. He told me that they had just received a Model Y shipment; the 3s were on their way. Asked about what lay behind the curtain in Tesla wonderland, he said that there were hundreds of cars “back there.”

Majella drove REDD home and I drove Tess. I am having mixed feelings. I get attached to my cars; it was difficult to sell George (my ‘64 Wolseley) and Ruby (my Hyundai Accent). But they were old and tired and their time had come. Tess, at 180,000+ kilometres still feels young. It’s me that’s getting old. The letting go is being made easier because we are selling Tess to our youngest daughter. So, we will still be in contact with the car and watch the milestones as she grows.

As we sipped our celebratory champagne, I mused at the difference between buying the Model Y in 2026 and the Model 3 in 2019. Going from the Hyundai to the Tesla was a massive leap in both design and technology — the screen, the regen braking. Our Tesla was the only one in our suburb, and there was no high-speed charging. Electric vehicles were seen as a “soon to pass” fad on the way to hydrogen cars, and a stupid decision in a country as big as Australia. In 2019, less than one percent of new cars sold had a plug, Tesla was still on a deathwatch. We had taken a risk — would it work out?

It certainly has! Owning Tess and dealing with FUD gave me a cause to champion. I started exploring this new world and writing about it — driving long trips and proving that an EV can do what it has to. CleanTechnica published my ramblings — which have now reached over 1,000 articles. People contacted me and shared their stories of private ownership. CEOs of new startups (like recently introduced Thermal Dawn ) gave me interviews and insights. This might sound weird, but moving from the Model 3 to the Model Y is nowhere near as exciting. Yes, I will continue to write, but the motoring world has changed. In Australia, the Model Y has been the highest selling passenger car of all drivetrains for the past few months. In October, it even beat the refreshed Toyota RAV4. My northern Brisbane suburb is full of Tesla Model Ys. The crossover has become common.

Motoring journalists are learning slowly to accept the new kids on the block, and most of their reviews seem to indicate a modicum of tolerance and truth. Of course, we still have vested interests proclaiming that Chinese cars are destroying the Australian car industry . Read: dealerships can’t sell ICE cars and aren’t making enough money. I wonder sometimes what there will be left write about as plugins take more and more of the market, and “real” motoring journalists write the articles I normally write. Relax, I am sure there will be room for all of us for some time. Especially in the USA!

raw_title: You Officially Missed Your Chance To Buy A New Toyota Supra Or BMW Z4
title: You Officially Missed Your Chance To Buy A New Toyota Supra Or BMW Z4
raw_summary: We all knew this day was coming, but none of us wanted to face it; the MkV Toyota Supra and G29 BMW Z4 are officially off the new car market. Our friends at CarsDirect analyzed national dealer inventory data on Tuesday and found that there are no more new Supras or Z4s on dealer lots across the United States. Both models were built at the Magna Steyr contract manufacturing facility in Austria, but their production run concluded in spring of this year. At least both manufacturers commemorated the end of production with Final Editions, but we're still sad to see both nameplates join the great new car lot in the sky. For now, at least. Toyota Motor North America's senior vice president of product planning and strategy Cooper Ericksen told MotorTrend that a Supra successor is coming, but that there will be another hiatus in the iconic sports car's legacy. Ericksen said, "it is our goal to have a gap that is significantly less [than the last one]." That last gap between the fourth-generation Supra and the fifth-generation car lasted an excruciating 20 years, so hopefully the sixth-generation Supra comes much sooner than that. Sadly BMW has not publicly announced plans for a fourth-generation Z4 as of now.

Toyota Motor North America's senior vice president of product planning and strategy Cooper Ericksen told MotorTrend that a Supra successor is coming, but that there will be another hiatus in the iconic sports car's legacy. Ericksen said, "it is our goal to have a gap that is significantly less [than the last one]." That last gap between the fourth-generation Supra and the fifth-generation car lasted an excruciating 20 years, so hopefully the sixth-generation Supra comes much sooner than that. Sadly BMW has not publicly announced plans for a fourth-generation Z4 as of now.

The fourth-generation of BMW's Z4 hit the streets of a very different world eight years ago in 2019, and offered the classic long-nose, short-deck sports car design solely in ragtop form. The GR Supra debuted a year later in 2020, and caused quite a buzz among car enthusiasts for its Bavarian lineage, but quickly proved it was still true to the Supra formula as a powerful two-seat driver's car. BMW sold just 2,113 Z4s in 2025, and Toyota managed to shift slightly more Supras at 2,953, but neither figure is particularly impressive or cost effective, especially considering that pricey platform updates would be necessary to conform to changing regulations.

The automotive industry has been a bit unsteady as of late, affecting even industry stalwarts like BMW and Toyota. BMW slashed its outlook for 2026 in June , and typical sales leader Toyota just posted its third-straight month of sales declines despite simultaneously raising its annual earnings forecast.

Fortunately BMW isn't leaving driving enthusiasts out to dry, with the launch of its Neue Klasse vehicles including the highly anticipated iX3 electric crossover and a new iteration of the always titillating 3 Series sedan . Toyota isn't abandoning driving enthusiasts either, with a new Celica in the works. In the meantime, BMW has an array of performance cars including the excellent M2 , M3, and M4, and Toyota has the hilariously fun GR Corolla and GR86, but we'll still miss the Z4 and Supra.

raw_title: Saving The Manuals: Porsche's Mechanical MECOSA Vs. Ferrari's Electronic Manuale Tech
title: Saving The Manuals: Porsche's Mechanical MECOSA Vs. Ferrari's Electronic Manuale Tech
raw_summary: Sometimes even an exotic carmaker's answer to a challenge might say something about future cars for the proletariat. Most of us probably can't even afford a replacement shift knob on the 2027 $677,600 Ferrari 12Cilindri Manuale, but how Ferrari and Porsche are adapting their automatics to fit manual transmissions could one day portend stick-shifts for us all. Here's the reason to even posit this: Carmakers want a cheaper way to build hybrids, EVs, and gas cars on the same platform and on the same assembly line. Adding or subtracting parts will make that too costly — which may result in them just ditching any manual effort, if that's the only solution. Now that you understand the why of this reporting, we'll also acknowledge why some readers are freaking out about the fact that the 12Cilindri Manuale will simulate the experience of shifting. It's not a conventional manual, and we'll explain how it works in greater depth, but the gist is that Ferrari's linking an electric stalk and faux clutch pedal to an eight-speed dual-clutch drivetrain. It's as real (or fake) as paddle shifters, just via a dongle and pedal.

article_paragraphs: Sometimes even an exotic carmaker's answer to a challenge might say something about future cars for the proletariat. Most of us probably can't even afford a replacement shift knob on the 2027 $677,600 Ferrari 12Cilindri Manuale, but how Ferrari and Porsche are adapting their automatics to fit manual transmissions could one day portend stick-shifts for us all. Here's the reason to even posit this: Carmakers want a cheaper way to build hybrids, EVs, and gas cars on the same platform and on the same assembly line. Adding or subtracting parts will make that too costly — which may result in them just ditching any manual effort, if that's the only solution.

Now that you understand the why of this reporting, we'll also acknowledge why some readers are freaking out about the fact that the 12Cilindri Manuale will simulate the experience of shifting. It's not a conventional manual, and we'll explain how it works in greater depth, but the gist is that Ferrari's linking an electric stalk and faux clutch pedal to an eight-speed dual-clutch drivetrain. It's as real (or fake) as paddle shifters, just via a dongle and pedal.

On the other hand, Porsche's stick-shift retrofit is a hack of their seven-speed PDK, which stands for Porsche dual clutch– or Doppelkupplung. It debuted on the 2020 Porsche 911 Carrera S Manual, dubbed MECOSA, which is Porsche-speak for MEchanically COnverted Shift Actuator, and is an entirely mechanical retrofit, featuring a seven-speed gated shifter and third pedal. But which is better? And which foreshadows a future joystick for the masses?

Automatics have been steadily growing in popularity since their debut in 1939, and according to the U.S. Department of Energy, by 2022, 99% of all new cars sold offered automatics. Standard automatics further evolved in 1987, with the introduction of the gearless CVT — a transmission Jalopnik readers hate in a way that borders on irrational .

The alternative? Something like Porsche's PDK, which is a dual-clutch manu-matic. Porsche began experimenting with the PDK in the 1980s. It debuted in racing in the 1986 962, and by 2008 you could get a PDK in a 911, which allowed drivers to shift using paddles for extra engagement and provided benefits such as engine braking. But it does more than just ditch the third pedal and shifter — the PDK in the 2020 Carrera S shifts at least 200% faster than a human can shift in the MECOSA, according to Car and Driver .

Despite that, at least 20% of Porsche 911 customers in America opt for a genuine manual, hence the MECOSA. Mind you, this is still a PDK underneath, and since its gears are arranged for a computer to actuate, not a human, they're not in any sane order. Instead, the pattern looks like this, starting from the top left of the gate: R,2,3,1,6,4,5,7. To translate the driver's inputs into proper shifts behind the scenes, MECOSA activates a jangle of cables and shafts so that each push or pull of the shifter engages the correct gear.

It's a solution that would make MacGyver proud. It is also not one Porsche is sticking with. The Stuttgart giant isn't abandoning its 911 customers clamoring for a manual; but now, you can get a Carrera S with a standard six-speed transmission, rather than a seven-speed with a Rube Goldberg machine tacked on.

Like Porsche, Ferrari's Manuale has a gated shifter instead of paddles, and it gains a third pedal on the floor. The transmission is physically identical to that of the paddle-shift version. Ferrari's legerdemain is to delete the paddles, insert a shift knob, and add a clutch pedal with sprung feedback. Now it feels as if your left foot is encountering a clutch spring as your ankle hinges, and Ferrari has created similar tricks in the gated shifter itself to simulate the feeling of gear shifts. Behind the scenes, however, sensors track both inputs. Your motions tell the car's computers what to do, which is identical to what happens when you pilot the 12Cilindri minus the Manuale. Except, in this one, it's possible to encounter rough shifts and even to stall the Manuale.

article_paragraphs: School buses haven't changed much since 1939 , but they came a long way before then. Some of the first vehicles used to take kids to school were simply horse-drawn wagons. It wasn't until the start of World War I that the first motorized buses seem to have appeared in this country. That's when a company called Wayne Works introduced a model in 1914. It was built on a long-wheelbase Model T chassis, so its engine was in the traditional location, under the hood up front.

Fast-forward a few years and we find Crown Coach evolving the concept of motorized school buses even further. Crown was a major commercial-vehicle manufacturer, founded in 1903 to sell business wagons to businessmen. It would survive all the way up to 1990 by building not only buses, but also hearses, fire trucks, bakery trucks, ambulances, and even airplanes.

Crown brought some notable innovations to the bus field as well. For example, it introduced the forward-control school bus in 1932. This wasn't the first forward-control bus of any type in the country, though. A firm called Twin Coach has that honor. The company had already been building flat-faced delivery trucks, and during the Depression, it brought the layout to its small buses — including some meant for municipal transit.

The head start for flat-faced city buses meant that when flat-faced school buses became popular, folks looked back to the first application to name the second. The new wave of so-called transit-style school buses gave school districts a new way to transport kids, with both new advantages and new drawbacks compared to conventional school buses.

First off, let's deal with their industry classifications: Class C buses are conventional buses, with engines in front and the main exit/entrance located behind the front wheels. The flat-front buses are in Class D and can theoretically have their engines anywhere from beside the driver to the very back of the bus. In the real world, positioning the motor at the rear is a big-time benefit to driver and students alike. That way, they face less noise, heat, and air pollution.

The transit-style layout also improves the driver's vision, since there's no massive hood to see over and around. Conventional buses are more like those big pickups with huge frontal blind spots that just keep getting larger as the years go by. Additionally, the flat-face setup maximizes how many passengers can fit in a given footprint. The difference isn't huge, but the flat-face buses can generally fit up to 90 passengers while conventional versions max out at about 77 to 83.

For their part, the traditional buses tend to be more maneuverable than their alternatives. This is partly due to their different wheelbases and how they can change a vehicle's handling . Looking at data from the Bureau of Transportation, Class C conventional buses with a recommended wheelbase of about 21.3 feet have noticeably shorter turning radii than Class D transit-style models, with recommended wheelbases of 23 feet. Lower maintenance costs are another strong suit of the conventional buses, as it's much easier to access their engines.

In the end, the reason you'll see conventional buses in some places and transit-style versions elsewhere is a matter of local preference. But neither class is likely to save kids from traumatic school bus stories .

raw_title: Brazilian GP qualifying red flagged almost immediately due to rain
title: Brazilian GP qualifying red flagged almost immediately due to rain
raw_summary: Brazilian Grand Prix F1 2026 qualifying has been red flagged barely two minutes in for horrendous wet weather conditions. Rain was always a possibility and was forecast for Saturday at Interlagos, but torrential rain even as the session got underway caught out a host of cars and forced Formula 1 stewards into action. Eight cars: Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes, George Russell's Mercedes, Charles Leclerc's Ferrari, Isack Hadjar's Red Bull, the Alpines of Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto, Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin and the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas all ventured out on intermediate tyres, but almost as soon as the cars hit the track it became clear that the conditions weren't driveable. Replays showed Lando Norris almost crashing, and Antonelli and Hadjar both laughed at how ridiculous the conditions were, also expressing the need for waterproofs. Gabriel Bortoleto summed up the mood: "When I get out, I need to change my clothes, I'm completely wet!" Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton appeared to demonstrate their experience in F1 by not venturing out on track and remaining dry in the garage. There's no confirmed restart time yet as rain continues to pummel the track. Nico Hulkenberg was told the rain would fall this heavily for at least 10 minutes, with that radio message coming at 1808 UK time.

raw_title: The Reason Subaru Still Builds Cars With Boxer Engines
title: The Reason Subaru Still Builds Cars With Boxer Engines
raw_summary: Exceptional balance and low-slung performance make the boxer engine a Subaru hallmark, but tight packaging and tricky repairs are the price you pay. You might know that Subaru still builds cars with boxer engines, but have you ever wondered why? The off-beat burble you may know and love Subaru for may have been toned down since the days of the rally-winning GC8 Impreza, but when it comes to what's under the hood, you're still going to find a horizontally opposed engine.
summary: Exceptional balance and low-slung performance make the boxer engine a Subaru hallmark, but tight packaging and tricky repairs are the price you pay. You might know that Subaru still builds cars with boxer engines, but have you ever wondered why?
article_paragraphs: Exceptional balance and low-slung performance make the boxer engine a Subaru hallmark, but tight packaging and tricky repairs are the price you pay.

You might know that Subaru still builds cars with boxer engines, but have you ever wondered why? The off-beat burble you may know and love Subaru for may have been toned down since the days of the rally-winning GC8 Impreza, but when it comes to what's under the hood, you're still going to find a horizontally opposed engine.

First off, what is a boxer engine? Well, simply put, it's an engine with horizontally opposed cylinders, the movement resembles a boxer jabbing at their opponent. Because the cylinders of a boxer engine are horizontally placed, you may also know them as being referred to as "flat" engines. Now, Subaru didn't invent the boxer engine; The first one appeared in 1896 by Benz & Cie, a forefather of the company we now know as Mercedes-Benz.

Even without a historical connection per se, there's a reason why Subaru continues to employ them in its latest cars. According to Subaru, the symmetrical design of boxer engines reduces friction and vibration, resulting in smoother ride characteristics. Having driven my fair share of Subaru's, they really do have a unique character to them. Since a flat engine is, well, flatter than a conventional inline-four cylinder, it can be placed lower in the engine bay, enabling the vehicle to enjoy a lower center of gravity. Couple that lower center of gravity with Subaru's signature symmetrical all-wheel drive system, and you have a pedigree of cars that are great for performance driving.

While there are many advantages that boxer engines have over conventional inline engines, there are a few notable downsides. The first being the overall footprint. Sure, the flatter size helps lower the center of gravity, but they are notably wider and more complex than an inline or V-configuration engine, meaning that they offer automakers less flexibility with packaging.

Another drawback with boxer engines is accumulation of oil at low points, which, due to their configuration, can mean part of the cylinder heads. This means they may require more frequent head gasket replacements, and they are prone to oil starvation if revved from a cold start before the engine's oil has had a chance to properly circulate. For the same reason, the correct oil level must always be maintained in a boxer engine. Oil starvation was also why a lawsuit was filed in 2024 against the boxer-engine BR-Z and Toyota GR86 . Maintenance cost is yet another drawback. For starters, you've got two cylinder heads, which means two head gaskets and related components. Plus, due to the low-slung layout of the engine, something as trivial as a spark plug change will be more labor-intensive.

So has Subaru ever made a non-boxer engine? Well, while boxer engines have made up much of Subaru's line-up, this famous automaker has also made non-boxers. Perhaps the most commonplace of these are the in-line three-cylinder units used in Subaru kei cars and vans. Subaru also made a larger EF-series 1.2-liter engine for use in its Justy economy car of the '80s. While most of Subaru's four-cylinder portfolio remains horizontally opposed, the automaker did produce a straight four. Called the EN-series, it was also used in their R-2 and other kei cars up until 2012.

If you're seriously considering a Subaru, then it's important to know what some of the issues may be down the road. Subaru's boxer engines have a generally straight rep if maintained right. However, like all unusual and slightly quirky powerplants, and in my own experience, they may become fussy if ill-treated. One common flaw with many Subaru boxer engine series is oil consumption. This is because of low-tension piston rings that were fitted to improve fuel efficiency. Faulty crankcase ventilation systems can also cause this.

title: The Buick Engine That Helped Launch The SR-71 Blackbird
raw_summary: The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird spy plane is capable of flying 2,193.2 mph with a ceiling above 85,000 feet. To achieve those feats, it packed a pair of Pratt & Whitney J58 turbojets to enjoy a combined 50,000 pounds of thrust, and it even used a new kind of fuel that could withstand the friction from those blistering speeds. However, getting those mighty motors to turn over in the first place was no simple task, which is where the Buick Nailhead comes into play. It might not have directly powered the plane, but its earliest flights were only possible thanks to the engine. A turbine engine requires a certain amount of airflow to ensure the fuel first ignites properly, and it has to reach a certain speed before the combustion process can sustain itself. As a result, the turbojet engines need to begin spinning even before they're operating on their own. But these are massive mills weighing in at 6,000 pounds each, so a simple electric starter like the one in a traditional car wouldn't have the strength to get the job done. A pair of Buick engines, on the other hand, would be enough to give its turbines the power they needed.
summary: The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird spy plane is capable of flying 2,193.2 mph with a ceiling above 85,000 feet. To achieve those feats, it packed a pair of Pratt & Whitney J58 turbojets to enjoy a combined 50,000 pounds of thrust, and it even used a new kind of fuel that could withstand the friction from those blistering speeds.
article_paragraphs: The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird spy plane is capable of flying 2,193.2 mph with a ceiling above 85,000 feet. To achieve those feats, it packed a pair of Pratt & Whitney J58 turbojets to enjoy a combined 50,000 pounds of thrust, and it even used a new kind of fuel that could withstand the friction from those blistering speeds. However, getting those mighty motors to turn over in the first place was no simple task, which is where the Buick Nailhead comes into play. It might not have directly powered the plane, but its earliest flights were only possible thanks to the engine.

A turbine engine requires a certain amount of airflow to ensure the fuel first ignites properly, and it has to reach a certain speed before the combustion process can sustain itself. As a result, the turbojet engines need to begin spinning even before they're operating on their own. But these are massive mills weighing in at 6,000 pounds each, so a simple electric starter like the one in a traditional car wouldn't have the strength to get the job done. A pair of Buick engines, on the other hand, would be enough to give its turbines the power they needed.

The mill used to get the Blackbird's own engines spinning was a 401-cubic-inch Nailhead, which can pound out 325 horses and 445 pound-feet of torque. The Air Force used a pair of those motors on the Blackbird's original start cart, yoking them together with a 12-inch-wide belt joining their transmissions. The combined output was then fed to the jets via mechanical linkage, spinning them up to their proper running speed. The pilot would then ignite the engines, allowing the Blackbird to run on its own from there.

We've previously explained how the Buick Nailhead V8 got its name ; the tops of its vertically oriented valves looked like, well, nailheads. The first-gen motor from 1953 had a displacement of 322 cubic inches, and an example with 264 cubic inches came to be when the brand introduced the Buick Special the next year. That latter setup had a pretty short life, as it was out of production after 1955. The Nailheads then began their climb up the displacement ladder. From 1957 to 1961, Buick raised the bar to 364 cubic inches. There was also a 425-cubic-inch Nailhead V8 on the roster from 1963 to 1966, backed by 360 horsepower with its optional dual-quad carburetor setup.

The 401, though, was especially popular. Among the first cars with this engine under their hoods were the 1959 Buick Invicta and Electra. It's also worth noting that, in the Invicta, the motor gained the Wildcat 445 nickname for its impressive torque rating. The Invicta Wildcat that premiered in 1962 (and became the Buick Wildcat in 1963) relied on that mill to help boost the brand's performance credibility.

The striking first-generation Buick Riviera would boast the 401 Nailhead in 1963, as would the Skylark Gran Sport when it arrived in 1965. The Skylark GS represents the point where Buick went all-in on the 401's performance potential — at least from a marketing standpoint. Even though its engine's output was unchanged from previous Buicks, the Skylark GS is considered to be Buick's first muscle car. Production of the engine itself would meet its end by the next year, but its use in the Blackbird would continue for a much longer period of time.

The Buick Nailhead engines would go on to power plenty of dragsters, too, building a proven track record for delivering low-end torque. Remember, that Wildcat 445 exceeded a pound-foot of twist for every cubic inch of displacement. When you also consider the Nailhead's reputation for long-term reliability, it's no surprise that it worked so well on Blackbird duty.

Yet, after roughly a decade on the start cart, the Nailheads would be retired in the 1970s and replaced by two other power-packed GM V8 engines. These were 454-cubic-inch big-block LS7 V8s that had originally been engineered to bring 460 horses to the 1970 Chevrolet Corvette. A combination of circumstances kept that motor out of regular production entirely, but that didn't prevent the Air Force from snagging a pair. (As a side note, those LS7 big-blocks were unrelated to the more recent LS7 Corvette engine that defied small-block limits in the C6 Z06.)

raw_summary: Esbjerg, Denmark, is using large electric heat pumps to extract heat from the North Sea and supply its district-heating network. During a two-hour winter test, seawater entered the system at 3.3°C and left at 1.2°C. The two heat pumps consumed 19.9 MW of electricity and supplied 55.2 MW of heat at a district-heating water temperature of 90°C. The difference, 35.3 MW, came from the seawater. The project team’s May 2025 operating report recorded a coefficient of performance, or COP, of 2.8. The figures describe that test, not annual average performance. A heat pump transfers thermal energy from a colder source to a warmer destination. Its refrigerant absorbs heat at a temperature below that of the seawater, and an electrically driven compressor raises the temperature so the heat can enter the district network. Esbjerg uses carbon dioxide as its refrigerant in a high-pressure cycle. For each unit of electricity used by the compressors during the test, the plant delivered 2.8 units of heat. Resistance heating would have required 2.8 times as much electricity for the same heat output under those conditions.

article_paragraphs: Esbjerg, Denmark, is using large electric heat pumps to extract heat from the North Sea and supply its district-heating network. During a two-hour winter test, seawater entered the system at 3.3°C and left at 1.2°C. The two heat pumps consumed 19.9 MW of electricity and supplied 55.2 MW of heat at a district-heating water temperature of 90°C. The difference, 35.3 MW, came from the seawater. The project team’s May 2025 operating report recorded a coefficient of performance, or COP, of 2.8. The figures describe that test, not annual average performance.

A heat pump transfers thermal energy from a colder source to a warmer destination. Its refrigerant absorbs heat at a temperature below that of the seawater, and an electrically driven compressor raises the temperature so the heat can enter the district network. Esbjerg uses carbon dioxide as its refrigerant in a high-pressure cycle. For each unit of electricity used by the compressors during the test, the plant delivered 2.8 units of heat. Resistance heating would have required 2.8 times as much electricity for the same heat output under those conditions.

The installation has a nominal heating capacity of 70 MW and began delivering heat in late 2024, as part of Esbjerg’s replacement of its retired coal-fired combined heat and power plant. The operating report describes controls for variable conditions and protection against freezing as seawater temperatures fall. The recorded COP of 2.8 was lower than the more favourable performance figures used in the original project expectations, and full guarantee testing had not been completed when the results were published. The city’s heating supply also includes a wood-chip boiler and waste-incineration heat. Emissions reductions reported for the wider replacement programme cannot be attributed in full to the seawater heat pumps.

Electricity price and heating-network temperature have a direct effect on the cost. At an illustrative electricity price of €100/MWh, compressor power at COP 2.8 costs about €36 per MWh of useful heat. That excludes seawater pumping, equipment maintenance, capital recovery, financing and heat distribution. A network able to operate at lower water temperatures generally asks the compressor to make a smaller temperature increase, which can improve COP. Older networks supplying 90°C heat face a harder operating requirement than newer, lower-temperature networks.

Esbjerg builds on decades of seawater heating experience. Monaco began using seawater heat pumps in 1963, and Stockholm has used large seawater-sourced district-heating equipment since the 1980s. Creative Energy’s Horseshoe Bay development in West Vancouver takes a different approach. Submerged heat exchangers transfer heat through a closed loop, with no seawater intake or discharge to the marina. Denmark’s Aalborg project is developing 177 MW of seawater heat-pump capacity. These installations serve different loads and use different marine arrangements, so their costs cannot be assumed to match Esbjerg’s.

Marine heat systems require more than suitable water temperatures. Engineers must address corrosion, biological fouling, intake and discharge effects, pumping requirements, maintenance access and freezing protection. The environmental assessment has to consider the local marine ecosystem and the discharge of colder water. The distribution network can be the larger financial obstacle in areas without existing pipes or concentrated heat demand. Wastewater, industrial waste heat, ground-source systems or individual air-source heat pumps may provide lower-cost heat at some sites.

Hot-water storage can add value by allowing a utility to make some heat when electricity is inexpensive and deliver it later. The available flexibility depends on storage capacity, network temperatures and heat demand. Esbjerg’s test provides direct evidence that cold seawater can support high-temperature district heating. Coastal utilities can use that evidence when comparing local heat sources, network investments and the costs of replacing combustion-based heating.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Esbjerg’s operating results, experience in Stockholm and Monaco, the Horseshoe Bay system near Vancouver, and the cost and environmental factors that determine where seawater heating is suitable.

raw_title: 4 Used Cars With Oil-Burning Engines That Consumer Reports Says To Avoid
title: 4 Used Cars With Oil-Burning Engines That Consumer Reports Says To Avoid
raw_summary: For any savvy driver reluctant to cough up the eye-wateringly steep new-car asking prices today, a used car seems like a no-brainer option. However, buying a used car can be a minefield, too. Inspect the car too casually, and you could be flirting with unreliability. Luckily, the non-profit organization Consumer Reports (CR) helps buyers identify the vehicles that are much more likely to suffer unexpected faults or hidden issues — like burning oil in the case of gas-powered cars. For those wondering, your car burning oil means oil is getting into the combustion chamber where it gets burned along with the air-fuel mixture. And since oil is essential for lubrication, cooling, and protecting the internal components inside the engine, your car burning or using too much oil can have serious consequences for its longevity. Naturally, this problem will cause oil levels to run low, reducing the lubrication inside the engine — also known as oil starvation . Without an effective lubrication film, the friction between moving parts inside the engine can accelerate wear on critical components, which can ultimately result in complete engine failure.

article_paragraphs: For any savvy driver reluctant to cough up the eye-wateringly steep new-car asking prices today, a used car seems like a no-brainer option. However, buying a used car can be a minefield, too. Inspect the car too casually, and you could be flirting with unreliability. Luckily, the non-profit organization Consumer Reports (CR) helps buyers identify the vehicles that are much more likely to suffer unexpected faults or hidden issues — like burning oil in the case of gas-powered cars.

For those wondering, your car burning oil means oil is getting into the combustion chamber where it gets burned along with the air-fuel mixture. And since oil is essential for lubrication, cooling, and protecting the internal components inside the engine, your car burning or using too much oil can have serious consequences for its longevity. Naturally, this problem will cause oil levels to run low, reducing the lubrication inside the engine — also known as oil starvation . Without an effective lubrication film, the friction between moving parts inside the engine can accelerate wear on critical components, which can ultimately result in complete engine failure.

It's not just the engine either; excessive oil consumption can also lead to spark plug fouling – a condition where the spark plug becomes coated in oil deposits — resulting in engine misfires, reduced performance, and decreased fuel efficiency. Not to mention, the contamination from burned oil residue can find its way into the catalytic converter and clog it. Thankfully, choosing the right car helps you to avoid this problem. To that end, we reviewed Consumer Reports' list of used cars that burn oil to avoid, and what to go for instead.

The second-generation Chevrolet Equinox and the mechanically identical GMC Terrain are both likely to attract you if you're after a sharply styled compact crossover SUV that's commendably spacious and comfortable. Both offer expandable rear passenger room, lots of storage bins, and numerous tech features. Cargo space is also something that GM was unwilling to compromise on, with the Equinox offering 31.4 cubic feet of space with all seats in use and up to 63.7 cubic feet with the rear seats folded down.

If you considered the 2010-2013 Equinox back when it was new, you had two powertrain options: a standard 2.4-liter inline four-cylinder with 182 horsepower or a more potent 3.0-liter V6 producing 264 horsepower and 222 lb-ft of torque. However, for all of its reasonable output, owners of the 2.4-liter four-cylinder have been left with oil consumption issues, with numerous owners on Carcomplaints.com reporting oil burn issues, including the engine's tendency to burn through 3-4 quarts each month. Because of this, Consumer Reports recommends buying the 2010-2015 Toyota RAV4 instead, which gets many things right, including a roomy interior, good fuel efficiency, agile handling, and excellent reliability.

The epitome of German engineering excellence, the enduring BMW M5 has defined the sports sedan segment for decades. The fact that it blends predictable braking performance, pinpoint steering accuracy, dynamic handling, and supple ride quality without compromising on everyday practicality makes it a rational proposition for many enthusiasts. At the heart of the M5 F10 is an S63 twin-turbocharged 4.4-liter V8 engine generating 560 hp and 500 lb-ft of torque. Thanks to this, it can hit 60 mph in 4.1 seconds, according to BMW's estimate.

However, even a colossal performance car with plenty of attitude and ability can suffer oil-burning issues. In its 2014 reliability survey, Consumer Reports found the twin-turbo V8 in the F10 M5 to be the worst oil-burning engine on the list, with more than half of respondents reporting oil consumption issues with their vehicle. Consequently, CR heartily recommends opting for the 2013-2015 Lexus GS to anyone looking to buy a luxury sports sedan, even if it isn't quite as powerful as the M5. The GS offers a choice of two engines, the standard of which is a naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 producing 306 horsepower and 277 lb-ft of torque. The second engine is a hybrid setup comprising a 3.5-liter V6 that combines with an electric motor to generate 338 horsepower and 254 lb-ft of torque.

If you need an SUV that's set up to be comfortable while being sporty and practical, the 2010-2013 Acura MDX may seem like a no-brainer buy. And it is. It stands out in the midsize luxury crossover SUV segment with capable handling, a good mix of high-quality materials and craftsmanship, as well as up to 83.5 cubic feet of cargo space. It also has just about enough power to help you get around. Its 3.7-liter V6 makes 300 horsepower and 270 lb-ft of torque, with the sprint from 0-60 mph requiring 7.1 seconds.

title: GM Steps On Tesla's EV Toes With EV1 Celebration
raw_summary: In a move that shocked and surprised nobody, last week Tesla CEO Elon Musk pulled the plug on his much-hyped Cybertruck . Production will end sometime next year. It may be small consolation, but at least the Cybertruck sold more units than another notorious flop in modern automotive history, General Motors’s ill-fated EV1 sedan. Was EV1 really a flop, though? In sales, yes, but GM wants everyone to know that the EV1 beat Tesla to the electrification punch in key technology milestones. GM actually sold few, if any, EV1 units , preferring to lease the car with a focus on drivers in California. Production began in 1996 but that didn’t last long. In 2003 GM pulled the plug, recalled the vehicles, and sent them to the crusher, having produced barely more than 1,000 units overall.

It may be small consolation, but at least the Cybertruck sold more units than another notorious flop in modern automotive history, General Motors’s ill-fated EV1 sedan.
article_paragraphs: In a move that shocked and surprised nobody, last week Tesla CEO Elon Musk pulled the plug on his much-hyped Cybertruck . Production will end sometime next year. It may be small consolation, but at least the Cybertruck sold more units than another notorious flop in modern automotive history, General Motors’s ill-fated EV1 sedan. Was EV1 really a flop, though? In sales, yes, but GM wants everyone to know that the EV1 beat Tesla to the electrification punch in key technology milestones.

GM actually sold few, if any, EV1 units , preferring to lease the car with a focus on drivers in California. Production began in 1996 but that didn’t last long. In 2003 GM pulled the plug, recalled the vehicles, and sent them to the crusher, having produced barely more than 1,000 units overall.

Only a scant few escaped the junkyard. One of them was rescued by US filmmaker Alex Gibney, leading to his advisory role in the searing 2006 EV1 documentary “Who Killed the Electric Car?” (btw, Gibney ‘s newly released “Musk” documentary is available on streaming now).

This year marks the 30th anniversary of EV1 production, and GM is using the occasion to celebrate. Rather than shoveling all memory of the EV1 debacle into the memory hole, GM has embarked on sort of under-the-radar public relations campaign, seeking to position the car as a necessary, albeit short lived, step along the vehicle electrification journey.

In not so many words, GM also draws attention to the fact that its work on EV1 predates the launch of Tesla Motors, which came on the scene in 2003. The automaker’s Senior Writer and Editor at GM News, Chris Perkins, ran down the particulars in March, noting that EV1 was the first EV to deploy heat pumps for climate control, energy efficiency, and battery temperature management.

Perkins also takes note of the car’s regenerative braking system. “Engineers developed a system for the car that translated a driver’s brake-pedal input into an electronic signal that blended regenerative and friction braking,” Perkins wrote.
“It’s a precursor to the braking systems used in GM’s modern EVs, which also add One-Pedal Driving1 and paddle-actuated Regen-On-Demand2 capability,” he added.

EV1 also eschewed mechanical actuators in favor of fully electronic (aka by-wire) controls for the accelerator pedal, brake pedal, parking brake, and gear selector, with the power steering featuring electro-hydraulic control.

raw_title: Why The Nissan VQ35 Is One Of The Most Dependable V6s Ever
title: Why The Nissan VQ35 Is One Of The Most Dependable V6s Ever
raw_summary: One of the most loved Japanese sports cars of the 21st century is the Nissan 350Z, partly because it was one of the badass villain cars in "The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift." But there's more to it than just that. While looks are subjective, it's hard to deny that it has aged rather nicely. It's also still genuinely affordable, making it one of the cheaper alternatives to Japanese performance cars that have skyrocketed in value . But perhaps the main reason for its celebrated status is its engine: Nissan's VQ35. In essence, it's a 3.5-liter naturally aspirated V6 that produces around 287 horsepower in early 350Zs (or closer to 300 hp in the Nismo versions). Even by today's standards, the 350Z is quick: in Car and Driver 's testing, 0 to 60 miles per hour took 5.4 seconds, and it didn't top out until 156 mph. That's fast enough to red-face some of the greatest sport sedans of all time .

article_paragraphs: One of the most loved Japanese sports cars of the 21st century is the Nissan 350Z, partly because it was one of the badass villain cars in "The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift." But there's more to it than just that. While looks are subjective, it's hard to deny that it has aged rather nicely. It's also still genuinely affordable, making it one of the cheaper alternatives to Japanese performance cars that have skyrocketed in value .

But perhaps the main reason for its celebrated status is its engine: Nissan's VQ35. In essence, it's a 3.5-liter naturally aspirated V6 that produces around 287 horsepower in early 350Zs (or closer to 300 hp in the Nismo versions). Even by today's standards, the 350Z is quick: in Car and Driver 's testing, 0 to 60 miles per hour took 5.4 seconds, and it didn't top out until 156 mph. That's fast enough to red-face some of the greatest sport sedans of all time .

The good news doesn't stop there either, because the VQ35 is also famed for its reliability, despite oil consumption issues. As with anything mechanical, it does depend on how well you treat and maintain it, but do so properly, and you're likely in for one hell of an ownership experience.

Nissan made a few sound decisions right off the bat, like opting against turbocharging and keeping the engine naturally aspirated. (Of course, a naturally aspirated engine has fewer moving parts and is therefore generally considered better for durability.) The VQ35 also uses timing chains rather than timing belts. Timing chains are generally considered to be more durable than timing belts – they don't have a defined replacement period and can often last as long as the engine itself.

Thanks to a crankshaft and connecting rods made of forged steel, the VQ35 can deal with high-RPM loads and long-term wear and tear better than engines that use regular cast-metal internals. On top of that, the engine block and cylinder heads are made from aluminum alloy, which is famous for both its thermal conductivity and its resistance to corrosion. The pistons are also coated with a molybdenum-based lubricant, which helps reduce friction.

Aside from the 350Z, another notable host of the VQ35 is the Skyline. No, we're not talking about Nissan's most famous performance car ever , but about the subtle sedan that began life in 2001 as the 11th-generation Skyline, and eventually spawned a sportier GT-focused version called the 350GT. In North America, it was sold under the Infiniti badge.

Other famous Nissans to use the VQ35 include the second-generation Stagea 350RX, which is arguably one of the best wagons of all time , and the Nissan Maxima , which used this superb engine right up to its final model year (2023). You might also be interested to know the VQ35 made its way into several racing cars, albeit with some major alterations. Those include the 2009 Renault Megane Trophy and even Dallara's T05 and T08 open-wheel cars from the Formula Renault 3.5 Series. So, gained some more respect for this old buster?

title: Tesla deemed liable for fraud after Solar Roof 'experiment' on a home
raw_summary: A California judge has deemed Tesla liable for fraud in a Solar Roof lawsuit, after the company repeatedly failed to hand over evidence. Tesla had already admitted it breached the contract, broke its warranty, and was negligent on the job. The homeowner says fixing the damage will cost “well over $2.5 million.” Tesla once offered him $5,000.
summary: A California judge has deemed Tesla liable for fraud in a Solar Roof lawsuit, after the company repeatedly failed to hand over evidence. Tesla had already admitted it breached the contract, broke its warranty, and was negligent on the job. The homeowner says fixing the damage will cost “well over $2.5 million.” Tesla once offered him $5,000.
article_paragraphs: A California judge has deemed Tesla liable for fraud in a Solar Roof lawsuit, after the company repeatedly failed to hand over evidence. Tesla had already admitted it breached the contract, broke its warranty, and was negligent on the job.
The homeowner says fixing the damage will cost “well over $2.5 million.” Tesla once offered him $5,000.

The case is Conroy v. Tesla , filed in 2022 in San Diego Superior Court’s North County division (case No. 37-2022-00043670). Electrek reviewed the court orders, the complaint, and the parties’ joint trial readiness report. Here’s what’s in them.

Ambrose Conroy, who lives in Rancho Santa Fe, signed up for a Tesla Solar Roof in March 2020. The original contract was $82,210 for a 13.1 kW system. By February 2021, after two amendments, it had grown to roughly $110,000 for an 18.2 kW roof and six Powerwalls.
The roof was never finished. It never passed a county inspection, and it never produced a single kWh for the house.
Tesla isn’t contesting most of that anymore. In the joint report filed by both sides last month, Tesla stipulated to liability on three of the five claims.
The other two claims, fraud and negligent misrepresentation, are where things went badly for Tesla.

Judge Cynthia Freeland sanctioned Tesla twice over discovery before going further. She ordered it to pay $15,467.50 in February and another $13,500 in June, both times for failing to produce a proper privilege log and responsive documents, and both times warning that issue sanctions could follow.

raw_title: This Focus RS Makes Us Nostalgic for a Time When Ford Built Cars Besides the Mustang
title: This Focus RS Makes Us Nostalgic for a Time When Ford Built Cars Besides the Mustang
raw_summary: Ford killed off the Focus globally just last year, much to the chagrin of anyone who enjoyed a scrappy little hatchback or sedan with a blue oval up front. Sure, the Mustang is still around, but the Focus and the Fiesta provided an entirely different kind of Fast Ford, compact performance that you could use every day. And there was one Focus trim that was the best of them all. Here’s a nearly new example of maximum Focus: a 2016 Focus RS with just 2200 miles on the odometer, for sale on Bring a Trailer (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos). It’s a single-owner, garage-kept car from Texas, and for those in colder climes, it happens to have been optioned with the RS2 package that includes heated seats and a heated steering wheel. Slap on a set of snow tires, and get ready to shred this upcoming winter.

Slap on a set of snow tires, and get ready to shred this upcoming winter.
See all results for used 2016 Ford Focus RS for sale near 20147

Pairing a 350-hp 2.3-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine with a six-speed manual gearbox and clever all-wheel drive, the Focus RS was basically Ford’s answer to the Subaru STI and the Mitsubishi Lancer EVO. WRC champion Colin McRae did spend quite a bit of time rallying in Fords, and that heritage was baked right into the RS, even if U.S. fans weren’t as broadly familiar with the world of rally.

For those who were, the RS was a revelation. The punchy four built boost quickly, and it somehow had far more turbo personality than when it appeared in the EcoBoost version of the Mustang. The all-wheel drive was even better, equipped with the ability to direct as much as 70 percent of the power to either outside rear wheel. With understeer thus banished, the RS could tear up a winding back road with a pace equal to far more expensive machines.

And yes, it came with Drift mode. Fully unlock this ability by switching off traction control, and the Focus RS can lay down Ken Block–style tire-smoking slides with ease. Not great for your tire budget, but huge fun nonetheless.

The only drawback was trying to get your hands on one when new, as dealers often tried to add considerable markup to the price tag. This example, painted a laid-back Stealth Gray, flies under the radar a bit and is just waiting for an owner who is going to pack on the miles.

In a low-key color, and with only hints of the performance peeking out from that hatchback shape in the form of a rear wing and blue Brembo brakes, this RS is a bit of an if-you-know-then-you-know car. It’s a real shame that Ford doesn’t sell anything like it anymore. On the other hand, that just makes this one that much more special.

title: 1992 Schuppan Porsche 962R: One Man's Plan to Put a Group C Race Car on the Street
raw_summary: If you’ve got a desperate desire to own a modern, 600-horsepower, Porsche-­based street-legal race car and have $1,620,000 to back up this peculiar day­dream, the line forms to the right for one of Vern Schuppan’s Porsche 962CRs. The good news is it will be a very short line in the United States, with room for only seventeen. (If you’ve got $1,620,000, there isn’t any bad news.)
summary: If you’ve got a desperate desire to own a modern, 600-horsepower, Porsche-­based street-legal race car and have $1,620,000 to back up this peculiar day­dream, the line forms to the right for one of Vern Schuppan’s Porsche 962CRs. The good news is it will be a very short line in the United States, with room for only seventeen.
article_paragraphs: If you’ve got a desperate desire to own a modern, 600-horsepower, Porsche-­based street-legal race car and have $1,620,000 to back up this peculiar day­dream, the line forms to the right for one of Vern Schuppan’s Porsche 962CRs.
The good news is it will be a very short line in the United States, with room for only seventeen. (If you’ve got $1,620,000, there isn’t any bad news.)

Schuppan, whose resume includes a victory at Le Mans in 1983, a bronze medal at the ’81 Indianapolis 500, and experience on the Formula 1 tour, plans to build 50 of these Team Schuppan 962s. That’s 962, as in Porsche Official Race Car, twice the winner at Le Mans and three times an IMSA season champion.

With all sorts of real and imagined race-cars-for-the-road getting serious ink these days, Schuppan has been doing in­stead of promising. The 47-year-old Aus­tralian has this Le Mans long-tailed 962 li­censed and fully certified for the road and, as this is written, is close to complet­ing the first of what is to be a limited se­ries of Team Schuppan 962CRs (the no­menclature is “C” for Group C and “R” for road) on the same basis but with unique “GT” bodywork and all the com­fort features one might expect for more than 1.5 million dollars.

Because this project has been commissioned by a Japanese outfit—Art Sport Division, a company that specializes in exotic machinery and is headed by Toshio Terada—most of them will be measured in yen, 220 million or there­abouts. The company says it will sell the first 50 worldwide, with seventeen head­ed for America. The red car shown on these pages is also destined for Japan, for the garage of Hiroyuki Miyake, a real-estate executive and Schuppan racing sponsor who want­ed a Le Mans racer with the minimum of modifications needed to make it street-­legal. A genuine Stuttgart-built 962 (number 962/123), it started life in IMSA with the Primus team. Schuppan rebuilt it as a Group C car with a British-made aluminum honeycomb chassis and took it to Le Mans in 1988, where it was driven by Brian Redman, Jean-Pierre Jarier, and Eje Elgh. It ran sixth for a while and fin­ished tenth. After competing in the Fuji 1000-kilometer race that year, the car was retired. When Schuppan began pon­dering the notion of a roadgoing 962 some twenty months ago, it was there at the back of the shop, a suitable case for treatment.

This is a real-life racer, currently designated as a 962R, and is the prototype for Team Schuppan’s road rockets, the first of which should roll out the doors in Octo­ber. The work done on this car will be ap­plied directly to the “CR” street car, which, unlike this “R” model, will have its nose and headlight area smoothed and finished. (Miyake’s enthusiasm has gen­erated two more orders for replicas of this Le Mans car, so Schuppan now has plans to build five of them in addition to the 50 street cars. They will sell for the same price as the more comfortably equipped GT version.)

All of the “production” models will have Schuppan’s own carbon-fiber monocoque chassis, developed for his 962 race cars, and carbon-fiber and Kevlar bodywork instead of the original Porsche panels, which are mostly fiberglass.

Driving a full-spec Group C car on normal roads should not be a problem—­if the pavement is smooth. But bringing one into compliance with all of the appli­cable regulations is something else. Rather more, in fact, than Vern Schup­pan and his friend and associate Howden Ganley (another ex-racer from Down Under and the man behind the Tiga race-car company) had thought when they embarked on the venture.

But confirmation came during third practice that both Hamilton and Leclerc would take a fifth ICE of the year in Brazil, automatically triggering a 10-place grid penalty.

Confirmation of Max Verstappen’s huge 30-place grid penalty also came as he’s taking a new ICE, exhaust, turbocharger and power unit ancillary component (within his allowance), which will mean he’ll start at the back of the grid regardless of where he qualifies.

title: 5 Prestigious International Car Shows Where Automakers Reveal New Models
raw_summary: Changing industry dynamics and the rise of livestreaming have led many physical conventions and events to either go away entirely (most notably the Geneva Motor Show and the E3 video game expo) or shift to digital formats (Apple's major product keynotes). Thankfully, a lot of traditional car shows have stuck around globally and remain among the most important entries on the calendar for automakers. article_paragraphs: Changing industry dynamics and the rise of livestreaming have led many physical conventions and events to either go away entirely (most notably the Geneva Motor Show and the E3 video game expo) or shift to digital formats (Apple's major product keynotes). Thankfully, a lot of traditional car shows have stuck around globally and remain among the most important entries on the calendar for automakers.

Setting up a pavilion at an auto show, especially a reputable and longstanding one, can be expensive, but it gives automakers a global platform to unveil brand-new production cars, showcase wild concepts and designs , and introduce new technologies to journalists, industry executives, and prospective buyers. It's also always fun to walk through the pavilions at a motor show and check out new cars up close and in the flesh.

While hundreds of automotive exhibitions and trade shows are held across the world every year, there's an upper echelon of car shows for which automakers save their best reveals. These include long-running motor shows like IAA Mobility, exhibitions of growing significance like Auto China and Auto Shanghai, and Monterey Car Week, which isn't a convention but a week-long series of prestigious automotive events.

The Paris Motor Show, also known as Mondial de l'Auto, is one of the world's oldest automotive conventions, dating all the way back to 1898. Held biennially in the French capital, the Paris Motor Show has historically been a major platform for the country's top domestic automakers — Renault, Peugeot, Citroen, and the like — to reveal their latest and greatest to the world.

These include the Peugeot 402 in 1935 (one of the first European cars to feature a curvy, streamlined design), the Renault 4CV in 1946 and Citroen 2CV in 1948 (both instrumental in bringing personal mobility to a post-World War II, cash-strapped France), the Renault 5 Turbo in 1978 (a raucous 160-hp mid-engined supermini), and more. Landmark introductions from non-French automakers include the Lamborghini Sesto Elemento in 2010 and the Ferrari 250 Europa GT in 1954, along with the Porsche Carrera GT concept and Koenigsegg CC8S in 2000.

The 2026 iteration of the Paris Motor Show was held in October, and prominently featured concept cars like an all-electric revival of the Citroen 2CV , the striking Alfa Romeo Cuorerosso, the Peugeot E-T16 and RCZ Vision, the Alpine A310 Vision, the Renault E-Space, and the Fiat Multiplay.

Germany's International Motor Show or Internationale Automobil-Ausstellung, now branded IAA Mobility, beats the Paris Motor Show by just one year to claim the title of the oldest surviving car show in the world. Throughout its 129-year history, the biennial event has been held in various German cities, including Frankfurt am Main, Berlin, Leipzig, Cologne, and Munich. In a similar vein to the Paris Motor Show, IAA Mobility serves as a major showcase for Germany's big automakers, like BMW, Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Audi, and Porsche.

Notable debuts at the IAA throughout history include the BMW 1500 in 1961 (it introduced the brand-saving Neue Klasse lineup), a concept version of the Volkswagen Golf GTI in 1975 (widely considered the forefather of hot hatchbacks), the Mercedes-Benz 190E 2.3-16 in 1983 (the record-breaking pioneer of sporty compact luxury sedans), the Audi RS6 Avant in 2007 (a super-cool V10-powered wagon), the Porsche 918 Spyder in 2013 (part of the holy trinity of hybrid hypercars), and many more.

raw_title: Lamborghini Gallardo’s Original Designer Polishes His Masterpiece
title: Lamborghini Gallardo's Original Designer Polishes His Masterpiece
raw_summary: Before it threw in the towel and decided to get in the luxury crossover game with the Urus, the Gallardo was Lamborghini's bestselling model. Careful input from parent company, Audi, meant a rip-roaring V-10 and all-wheel-drive grip, and Italian design house Italdesign clothed this in angular styling that merged supercar and stealth fighter into a great-looking machine. It wasn't the top-dog Lamborghini at the time, but it packed a punch. The initial work at Italdesign was done by none other than Fabrizio Giugiaro, son of the legendary Giorgetto. The Gallardo would later be polished by Luc Donckerwolke, but it seems like Fabrizio had a few finishing touches of his own to add. Thanks to Cavën Atelier, a Spanish engineering firm, Giugiaro Jr. has had a crack at reworking his 2003 original with modern tech and plenty of tweaks.

It wasn't the top-dog Lamborghini at the time, but it packed a punch.

The initial work at Italdesign was done by none other than Fabrizio Giugiaro, son of the legendary Giorgetto. The Gallardo would later be polished by Luc Donckerwolke, but it seems like Fabrizio had a few finishing touches of his own to add. Thanks to Cavën Atelier, a Spanish engineering firm, Giugiaro Jr. has had a crack at reworking his 2003 original with modern tech and plenty of tweaks.

The Hommage 26 starts with a donor Gallardo, similar to the Encor Series 1 Lotus Esprit restomod, which is then thoroughly reworked with carbon-fiber bodywork throughout. The front end resembles the original, but now incorporates modern lighting and pop-down headlights.

Like an old silhouette Trans-Am Audi, only the top sliver of the car is unchanged, with the same roofline and glass. Everything else is subtly reshaped, including a new rear fascia with massive rectangular exhaust pipes and integrated rear active aerodynamic panels like those you might find in a Pagani Huayra .

Under this new skin, the car's 5.0-liter V-10 now spins to 8500 rpm, producing either 533 hp in GT trim or as much as 552 in full-fat Performance spec. There’s active suspension, upgraded brakes, and the Hommage 26 rolls on 20-inch wheels.

Cost? The equivalent of a Dr. Evil-approved $1 million, plus you have to B.Y.O. Gallardo. That is an astounding amount of money for a restomod version of a non-V-12 Lamborghini, and it seems almost like a litmus test of just how much the restomod market boom will bear. Only 25 examples are planned to be built.

Perhaps more interestingly, Cavën Atelier positions the Hommage 26 not as a one-off, but as a potential series of cars that will see designers return to their work for upcoming reboots. The options here are endless: Ken Okuyama redoes the Ferrari Enzo ? A Camilo Pardo reworked first-generation Ford GT ? Even if the price tags will be out of reach, the designs will be interesting to see.

In the meantime, your standard Gallardo remains pretty accessible for how exotic it looks and drives. Put aside a little money for an Akrapovič exhaust, and enjoy it just as Giugiaro originally imagined.

title: Is The 'Five-Year Rule' For Tires Still True?
raw_summary: Tire age vs. tire mileage: here is the real truth behind the legendary five-year replacement rule. There's a popular saying that if your tires are over five years old, you should change them — even if the car they are mounted to doesn't drive that often. Today, it's pretty easy to check tire age: just look for the four-digit date code on the sidewall, and you'll know the week and year of manufacture.

article_paragraphs: Tire age vs. tire mileage: here is the real truth behind the legendary five-year replacement rule.

There's a popular saying that if your tires are over five years old, you should change them — even if the car they are mounted to doesn't drive that often. Today, it's pretty easy to check tire age: just look for the four-digit date code on the sidewall, and you'll know the week and year of manufacture.

However, the commonly quoted "five-year rule" was introduced decades back. Surely, tire tech has changed to allow for longer lifespans? The short answer is, the five-year rule may still hold in most cases, but even manufacturers are hesitant to cite it as a definitive cut-off. It turns out that, yes, there are situations where you might be able to stretch to six, seven years, or even more. However, after your tire crosses that five-year mark, you're best served keeping a vigilant eye on them.

Let's start with when you buy new tires. Just because they're new on the car doesn't mean they're newly made. When you're buying new rubber for your ride, you must select the freshest tires possible. This means that you should look for the ones that have been manufactured most recently. As a prime example, let's look at buying tires right now, in 2026. You'd do well to look at tires manufactured in the last three months — that's July through September. Going a bit further back is also okay, say, March or April.

But if you select a tire made in, say, late 2025, you've lost a year of life before it's even reached your hands. And remember, these are the tires that salespersons try to aggressively flog because they need to move them ASAP. It's not bad buying such a tire, but you should expect a discount when doing so.

If you're wondering what's so bad about aged tires, well, rubber ages with time. With that age comes the added risk of a potential blowout. As the rubber ages, in some cases tiny cracks can form that compromise the tire's integrity. These start on a microscopic level, but as time passes by, they become visible to the eye. If you see cracks on the sidewalls of your tires, it's time for a replacement, pronto, because one day, that tire is going to let go.

Tires do this due to how they're constructed and the materials they're made from. Tires are created by methods that include curing. These use compounds that age and break down over time due to thermo-oxidative degradation. Simply put, oxygen slowly breaks down the tire's rubber compound. But there are other factors that accelerate tire aging.

Tires also age faster in hot climates, so if you live in areas with plenty of sun and frequently drive on blisteringly hot tarmac, you should inspect your tires more often. But tires still age when sitting in a dark warehouse — just slower. The same applies to your spare tire, even if it's sitting cozy inside your vehicle's trunk. As for vehicles with exposed or underslung spare wheels that get exposed to sun, rain, dirt, and road grime, they need even more attention.

raw_summary: Like many automakers, Audi is listening to the backlash towards touch-sensitive controls. It’s been implementing subtle changes to its infotainment interface and other controls to improve the user interface, and we recently got a chance to try these updates in a 2027 Audi Q6 e-tron . The Q6 e-tron (and its A6 e-tron sedan stablemate) launched for the 2025 model year. After skipping the 2026 model year, the 2027 model-year examples of these EVs underwent changes to the steering wheel to incorporate more physical controls and to the MMI infotainment software to simplify the interface. Similar changes have been propagating across the Audi lineup since. To start, there are new physical scroll wheels on the two steering-wheel spokes. The one on the left spoke controls the digital gauge cluster and cycles through different screens, while the one on the right spoke is a volume knob. There are still haptic buttons on the new wheel, but they’re responsive, and we prefer this setup to the previous one, which had only touch-sensitive buttons. The wheels are both simpler to use and have a satisfying click.

Audi also says it simplified the menu structures and changed the appearance of the display of its MMI infotainment interface, seen both on the central display screen and in the digital gauge cluster. We found the system easy to operate, with quick responses to inputs on the touchscreen, and the new appearance makes the built-in software look and feel a bit more like Apple CarPlay, with larger icons and simple backgrounds. Some of the vehicle-settings menus are still complex, but day-to-day functions such as audio controls and navigation were logical enough to use. As is the norm these days, over-the-air updates mean that Audi is also adding new functions to the system, such as the newly available Spotify app that allows you to access the streaming service in the car’s system without tethering it to your phone.

We’d still skip the optional passenger display screen, which seems unnecessary and is somewhat limited in its functions. Plus, given the amount of screen real estate already present on the dashboard, the addition of a third, 10.9-inch screen makes the entire dash look like a screen. The passenger display is available as part of the $1800 Technology package on the Premium Plus trim, and it comes standard in the top Prestige trim.

Despite being raised on a steady diet of base-model Hondas and Toyotas—or perhaps because of it—Joey Capparella cultivated an obsession for the automotive industry throughout his childhood in Nashville, Tennessee. He found a way to write about cars for the school newspaper during his college years at Rice University, which eventually led him to move to Ann Arbor, Michigan, for his first professional auto-writing gig at Automobile Magazine . He has been part of the Hearst Autos team since 2016 and now lives in New York City.

title: Are These 9 Concepts And Sporty Coupés Pre-Ford Mustang Pony Cars?
raw_summary: History books love romantic tales, like the one where Lee Iacocca, father of the Mustang, was responsible for giving birth to a whole new category of vehicles: pony cars. Sure, he was behind the creation of the most popular such vehicle, but the pony car concept was in the brewing stage years before the first-gen Mustang Mk1. While not strictly pony cars, these concepts and production sporty coupés already flirted with the concept of an enthusiast-grade compact car. Of course, we don't mean to diminish Iacocca's genius.
